headline: Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams report deterministic algorithms for 3SUM in O(n^1.9992) time and all-pairs shortest paths in O(n^2.9995), refuting the two hardness conjectures that most conditional lower bounds inside polynomial time are stated against.

items.title: Oxygen fills the selenium vacancies and the p-contact falls to 104 Ω·µm
items.dek: Lei Sun and co-authors dosed single-layer tungsten diselenide — a semiconductor three atoms thick — with oxygen, and the resistance of the junction where metal meets semiconductor fell eighteenfold, from 1,869 to 104 ohm-micrometres.
items.why_it_matters: Injection resistance, not channel quality, is what has kept two-dimensional p-type transistors out of complementary logic: a contact in the thousands of ohm-micrometres swamps a 16-nanometre channel's own resistance, so the device is measuring its own contacts. At 104 ohm-micrometres the contact stops dominating, which moves the open question from mobility to whether a surface oxygen treatment survives the gate stack, the later anneals and extended bias.
items.background_md: Where a metal touches a semiconductor, the metal's electron wavefunctions leak into the semiconductor's band gap — metal-induced gap states — and pin the Fermi level there, leaving a Schottky barrier whose height barely responds to which metal you chose. In a bulk semiconductor you defeat that by doping the region under the contact hard enough that carriers tunnel through a thin barrier instead of climbing over it. A monolayer has no bulk to implant into: there are three atomic planes and an ion beam destroys all of them. So the contact, not the channel, sets the current.
items.deeper_md:
Two effects come from one treatment. Controlled oxygen doping reduces the population of selenium vacancies in the as-grown film, and hole mobility rises from 55 to 218.3 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, which the authors describe as approaching the theoretical limit. The same oxygen acts as a p-dopant, so the region under the metal becomes heavily hole-doped and the Schottky barrier gets thin enough to tunnel through rather than being lowered. The resulting 16-nm-channel pFET delivers 1,635 µA µm⁻¹ saturation current at a drain bias of −1.2 V with a ballistic ratio of 81 % at room temperature.

For scale: a separate modelling study by Xiong and co-authors puts the quantum limit for p-type WSe₂ contacts just under 100 Ω·µm and proposes topological semimetal electrodes as the route there. So 104 Ω·µm sits at the edge of what the interface physics allows, not merely well below where everyone else is. Lain-Jong Li co-authored both papers, so read that framing as the same community's, not as an independent check.

Caveat: every figure above is from the abstract. The doping recipe, the device-to-device spread, and any thermal or air-stability data are in the methods and supplementary material, which this brief did not read — and record 2D device numbers have a long history of coming from one hand-made device on one good flake.

glossary.definition: Contact resistance normalised to contact width, so devices of different sizes compare; it adds in series with the channel, and once it exceeds the channel resistance the transistor is measuring its own contacts.
Electron states the metal pushes into the semiconductor's forbidden energy gap at the interface, which pin the Fermi level so the Schottky barrier height stops tracking the metal's work function.
The fraction of the current a device delivers relative to the limit in which carriers cross the channel without scattering once; 81 % means almost all carriers traverse 16 nm collision-free.
A missing Se atom in the WSe₂ lattice; it leaves a charged defect that scatters holes and donates electrons, which is why as-grown films are reluctant to behave as p-type.

items.fab_angle: The number that matters here is extracted, not measured directly: contact resistance comes from a transfer-length-method structure — a row of pads at increasing spacing, fitted to total resistance versus gap. That structure is within reach of a teaching cleanroom and a probe station, and it is the cheapest way to find out whether a new metallisation is working before anything else is blamed.

items.title: In silicon nitride the deepest traps are made by the electron that falls in
items.dek: Jonathon Cottom and Emilia Olsson computed electron capture at 415 sites in amorphous silicon nitride — the film that holds the charge in 3D NAND flash — and found that the deepest traps do not exist until an electron arrives and breaks a silicon–nitrogen bond behind it.
items.why_it_matters: A trap you can count in a fresh film is a defect to be engineered out of the deposition; a trap the write operation creates is a property of the write. If more than half of four-fold silicon sites convert on capture, then trap density is a function of how many electrons a cell has seen, and retention and read-disturb margin stop being bounded by film quality alone — which is the measurement most process work on nitride is set up to improve.
items.background_md: A flash cell stores a bit as electrons parked in an insulator above the channel, and in 3D NAND that insulator is amorphous silicon nitride. It is chosen because its disordered network carries a high density of deep localised electronic states — above 10¹⁹ per cubic centimetre — and depth is what buys retention: a state a few tenths of an electronvolt below the conduction band empties thermally in seconds, one a full electronvolt down holds for the ten years a datasheet promises. Which structural motifs supply those deep states is still contested.
items.deeper_md:
The calculation pairs a relaxed neutral cell with the same cell carrying one extra electron, 415 pairs of 280-atom Si₁₂₀N₁₆₀ structures built by melt–quench and then relaxed at the HSE06 hybrid-functional level in CP2K, and aligns the trap state before and after localisation so an electronic identity can be matched to a structural change.

Three routes coexist. 165 sites are polaronic: a four-fold silicon stays four-fold and an already-localised state tightens, median corrected stabilisation 1.17 eV. 65 are native K-centres, pre-existing silicon dangling bonds, at 1.33 eV. The interesting 182 start four-fold and end three-fold — the Si–N bond breaks on capture — at 1.47 eV. That third class is 44.2 % of classified traps but 69.0 % of the deepest spectral decile and 71.4 % of the top stabilisation decile.

Caveats, and they are large: 0 K, no hydrogen in the cells, electrons only, a single −1 charge state, 40 of 455 pairs discarded for artefacts, and no direct experimental comparison of the fingerprints. The hydrogen omission matters because Wilhelmer and co-authors report that K-centres persist in hydrogenated films despite hydrogen being the standard passivant, so passivation is unlikely to close the route this work identifies.

glossary.definition: A silicon atom in silicon nitride bonded to only three nitrogens, leaving one unpaired electron on a dangling bond; it is the canonical deep trap in the material and shows up in electron spin resonance.
A flash cell that stores electrons in localised states inside an insulating nitride layer rather than on a conducting floating gate, so a single leakage path drains one trap instead of the whole bit.

A screened hybrid density-functional approximation that mixes in part of the exact exchange interaction; it is used here because ordinary functionals underestimate band gaps and so misplace trap depths.

How far the system's energy drops when the electron localises at a site, after corrections for the periodic cell's spurious self-interaction; deeper means harder to empty thermally, so longer retention.

items.fab_angle: Nitride deposited by plasma CVD is a staple passivation and gate dielectric in a teaching fab, and the usual way to characterise it is a capacitance–voltage sweep before and after bias stress. If charge injection creates part of its own trap population, a pre-stress measurement does not bound the post-stress one, and the honest characterisation is a stress sequence with a C–V after each step rather than one before and one after.

sources.title: State aligned graph wavelet fingerprints of electron trapping in amorphous Si3N4

items.title: A relaxed oxygen divacancy flips which hafnia phase is easier to reach
items.dek: Hyunjin Lee and co-authors let a fully charged oxygen divacancy in hafnium dioxide relax instead of holding it in an idealised geometry, and the barrier toward the polar phase that makes the oxide ferroelectric became the lower of the two, 15.3 against 26.9 millielectronvolts per formula unit.
items.why_it_matters: Oxygen vacancies have been credited with stabilising ferroelectric hafnia thermodynamically, and a thermodynamic account predicts an equilibrium phase fraction you can only change by changing composition or stress. A kinetic account predicts something different and more useful: that anneal ramp rate and dwell time pick the phase, because a barrier difference of eleven millielectronvolts per formula unit only matters while the structure is still choosing. Those are knobs a furnace already has.
items.background_md: Hafnium dioxide has been the gate insulator in logic since the 45-nanometre node, and it became interesting a second time when thin films of it turned out to be ferroelectric — a switchable electric polarisation in a material every fab already runs. The polarisation comes from one specific crystal structure, the polar orthorhombic phase, and that structure is not the ground state: monoclinic hafnia sits about 84 millielectronvolts per formula unit lower and is non-polar. So a useful film means arriving at a metastable phase and staying there, which is why dopants, deposition stress and oxygen vacancies are all suspects.
items.deeper_md:
The system is a c-axis oxygen-divacancy complex in the tetragonal lattice, fully charged, in a 96-atom Hf₃₂O₆₄ supercell — a 3.125 % vacancy concentration — using VASP with PBE and projector-augmented waves at a 600 eV cutoff. The search scales each vacancy's neighbour distances by 1+δ with δ from −60 % to +60 % in 10 % steps, and finds a family of configurations 18.4 meV/f.u. below the idealised reference, reached without a barrier.

The reference and the relaxed structure then take solid-state nudged-elastic-band paths to monoclinic and polar orthorhombic with cell-relaxed endpoints. From the idealised reference the barriers are 6.9 meV/f.u. to monoclinic and 10.1 to polar orthorhombic, so monoclinic wins. From the relaxed family they become 26.9 and 15.3, and the ordering reverses — the monoclinic barrier nearly quadruples while the polar one grows by half.

Caveats: 0 K, no electric field, a uniform compensating background charge rather than real screening, only the fully charged state, and no experimental test. Note also the scale — the whole reversal turns on a difference of 11.6 meV/f.u., against about 26 meV of thermal energy at room temperature, so this is an ordering of rates in a regime where both paths are thermally reachable rather than one path being shut. The vacancy explanation is itself contested — Song and co-authors, working on doped epitaxial films, conclude that deposition stress dominates polar-phase stabilisation and that lattice strain effects are much smaller than changes in phase fraction. Shi Liu co-authored both this work and the 2021 paper that argued vacancies act thermodynamically, so this is a group revising its own account.

glossary.definition: Millielectronvolts per formula unit, here per HfO₂; it is an energy normalised per chemical unit so cells of different size compare, and room temperature is about 26 meV for scale.

The Pca2₁ structure of hafnia, whose unit cell has no inversion symmetry and therefore carries a permanent electric polarisation that an applied field can reverse; it is the only phase that makes the oxide ferroelectric.

A method that drags a chain of intermediate structures between two endpoints until it relaxes onto the lowest-energy path, giving the barrier height; the solid-state variant lets the unit cell shape change along the way too.

Two missing oxygen atoms in the lattice, here aligned along the c axis with one oxygen left between them; each vacancy can hold a charge, and the charge state changes which distortions around it are stable.

items.fab_angle: If phase selection is kinetic rather than thermodynamic, then the tube furnace recipe is the experiment: the same film ramped at different rates should land at different polar fractions. That is a measurable claim with a cheap read-out — polarisation–voltage hysteresis on a capacitor stack, or just the remanent charge — and it is the kind of result a club with a furnace and a probe station can argue with.

items.title: The offset trim is stored in the transistor doing the converting
items.dek: Jeries Mattar and co-authors built a voltage-to-time converter — a circuit that turns an analogue voltage into a pulse width — in GlobalFoundries 28-nanometre CMOS, and trimmed its input offset by partially switching the ferroelectric transistor that performs the conversion.
items.why_it_matters: Offset trim normally costs a separate digital-to-analogue converter, somewhere to keep its code, and a re-trim at every power-up, which is why a trim network can be larger than the circuit it corrects. Folding the trim into the converting device's own ferroelectric polarisation makes it non-volatile and area-free: the whole converter is 6.07 square micrometres, and across simulated process corners and ±10 % supply the offset is pulled inside 10 millivolts and the gain inside 4 %.
items.background_md: Supply voltages have barely fallen for a decade while the smallest time interval a digital gate can resolve has kept improving with each node, so analogue circuits increasingly move the signal out of voltage and into time: rather than compare two voltages, turn a voltage into a delay and compare edges. Resolution then scales with the process instead of against it. The price is that delay through a current-starved inverter depends on process corner, supply and temperature, so every such converter needs its offset and gain trimmed before the number it produces means anything.
items.deeper_md:
The converter is a clocked current-starved inverter with a 3-bit capacitor bank and an output inverter. Delay is C_B·ΔV_TRIP/(I_leak + I_FE(V_in)) — the input drives the gate of a 450 nm ferroelectric FET whose drain current discharges the bank, so a higher input discharges faster and the pulse gets narrower. Partially switching that FET's ferroelectric layer with a sub-full-swing erase pulse (+4 V to program, then 0 to −4 V to erase) sets a multilevel threshold state; 32 states in steps of 1/31 move the transfer curve's midpoint from 0.40 V to 0.66 V, a 260 mV trim range.

Centring it helps measurably: integral nonlinearity goes from +1.27/−2.42 to +0.65/−0.92 LSB at 5-bit, and second-harmonic distortion from −12.5 dB to −32.2 dB at 10 MS/s.

The caveats are in the paper. Measured ENOB is 2.0 bit, because near zero offset noise and not distortion is the limit: pulse-width noise measures 0.38 ns against 4.5 ps in simulation, 84×, which the authors attribute partly to supply noise on the leaker bias absent from the model. The 500 MS/s, 2.0 µW, 0.90 V design point is simulation only. Multilevel states are shown separated after 24 h at 85 °C, and GlobalFoundries' own 28 nm FeFET work reports retention to 10⁵ s with endurance above 10³ cycles — enough for a trim written once at wafer test, and not enough for a trim the chip would want to adjust in the field.

glossary.definition: Integral nonlinearity: how far a converter's transfer curve bends away from the straight line through its endpoints, measured in least-significant-bit steps, so 1 LSB of INL means a whole code of error.

Second-harmonic distortion — the power at twice the input frequency relative to the fundamental, in decibels; it is the signature of an asymmetric transfer curve, which is exactly what an uncorrected offset produces.
Effective number of bits: the resolution a converter actually delivers once its own noise and distortion are counted, as opposed to the number of codes it nominally outputs.
A ferroelectric layer only partly switched, so some domains point one way and some the other; the net polarisation sets an intermediate threshold voltage that persists without power.

items.title: Make the DDR5 command set extensible and in-DRAM compute can ship
items.dek: The SAFARI group at ETH Zürich and Carnegie Mellon proposes Terracotta, a DDR5 interface that lets a DRAM vendor define its own commands inside one standard encoding space, paired with a memory controller programmed from three primitives after the silicon exists.
items.why_it_matters: In-DRAM copying, subarray parallelism and latency-reduction schemes have accumulated in the literature and stayed in simulators, because each one needs commands the JEDEC interface does not define plus controller logic nobody will build for a single feature. Retaining above 96 % of a hand-built implementation's benefit purely by configuration is the argument that the command interface, not the DRAM array, was the thing standing in the way — and it is checkable, because two techniques composed under Terracotta beat either alone.
items.background_md: A DRAM chip is almost entirely passive. Opening a row, reading a column, precharging, refreshing — each happens because a memory controller drove one of a fixed set of command encodings across the bus, and that set is frozen by a JEDEC standard which every controller, chip and module in the industry is built against. Research that wants the array to do something new, such as copying a row internally or activating two subarrays at once, therefore needs a command that does not exist. That means a standard revision, new controller silicon, and everyone agreeing at the same time.
items.deeper_md:
Two pieces. Custom command extensions give vendors a defined space to declare new commands inside the single standardised interface, so the interface changes once rather than per technique. The controller is then built from three composable primitives — a trigger that detects a condition in the memory traffic, an update that changes controller state, and an action that issues commands — which is enough to express the control logic the existing proposals need.

Four techniques from four domains were ported: PRADA for processing-using-DRAM, MoPAC-C for cheaper maintenance, MASA for subarray-level parallelism and ChargeCache for latency reduction. All retain more than 96 % of their custom implementations' performance benefit, and the ChargeCache-plus-MASA composition beats either one alone. Overheads quoted on a server-grade processor are 0.6–3.2 % DRAM energy, 0.03 % area and 0.56 % power.

Caveat: this is Ramulator2 simulation across 65 workload traces, so the energy and area figures are model outputs, not measurements, and the primitives were chosen after looking at the four techniques they then express. The load-bearing assumption is also not technical. A vendor-extensible command space only buys anything if JEDEC standardises the extension mechanism and vendors publish their encodings, and no paper can deliver that. The work is accepted at MICRO 2026 and the artifact is public.

glossary.definition: The industry body whose DDR documents fix the exact command encodings, timings and pin assignments every DRAM chip and memory controller must obey; a technique needing a new command needs a new revision of that document.

A DRAM bank is cut into subarrays, each with its own row of sense amplifiers; they could in principle be activated independently, and exposing that is a standing way to buy parallelism without adding pins.

Doing copies or bitwise arithmetic by driving the array's own bitlines and sense amplifiers instead of hauling data to the processor, which saves bus traffic but needs commands the interface does not define.
The cycle-accurate DRAM simulator this evaluation runs inside; its timing, energy and area models — not hardware — produce every number in the paper.

items.title: 3SUM drops below n², and the APSP conjecture goes with it
items.dek: Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams report a deterministic algorithm that decides 3SUM — whether a list of n integers contains three that sum to zero — in O(n^1.9992) time — the first polynomial improvement on the quadratic bound — and the same primitive gives all-pairs shortest paths in O(n^2.9995).
items.why_it_matters: Hundreds of conditional lower bounds inside polynomial time are phrased as "this problem needs quadratic time unless 3SUM does not", and every one of them loses its hypothesis at once. What survives is the reductions themselves, which were always two-way: a web built to carry hardness outward from 3SUM now carries a speedup outward instead, and the problems that were declared closed become open again at a slightly smaller exponent.
items.background_md: Knowing a problem is in polynomial time does not tell you which polynomial, and for the problems that matter most the exponent has often not moved in decades. Fine-grained complexity handles that by naming a few problems whose best known running time is stuck — 3SUM at n², all-pairs shortest paths at n³, CNF satisfiability at 2ⁿ — assuming those times are optimal, and then reducing them into everything else. A reduction converts the assumption into a conditional lower bound: beat the target problem by any polynomial factor and you have beaten 3SUM too.
items.deeper_md:
The engine is a thin matrix product. Given an N×D matrix and a D×N matrix with D small, compute only a set of at most N²/√D wanted entries of the N×N product. Theorem 5 does that in O(N² log²D / D^(1/18)) operations on O(log N)-bit integers, for D a power of four and N ≥ D¹⁸; Theorem 1 restates it as O(N²/D^0.063) for D ≤ N^ε with ε < 0.1204 — polynomially faster than writing the product down, and faster than computing N²/√D inner products one at a time.

It works by recursion on Schönhage's ten-multiplication identity, which computes a 3×3 outer product and a 2×2 inner product together in 10 multiplications where 13 would be needed separately. Each input matrix is encoded once so the encoding cost is amortised across block multiplications, and the recursion tree is pruned to the leaves the wanted entries actually reach; bounding the union of those leaves is where the argument lives. Read as a graph problem, it solves all-edges sparse triangle on lopsided tripartite graphs in O(n^(2−0.063ε)).

What to watch. The authors say the hidden constants are enormous and the algorithms are "potentially impractical in their current form"; nothing improves for balanced sparse-triangle instances; the real-weight versions are Las Vegas randomised rather than deterministic. And it is a one-day-old preprint from two authors who built much of the theory it overturns, so the claim rests on the leaf-counting bound surviving other people reading it.

glossary.definition: Given n numbers, decide whether three of them sum to zero; sorting plus a linear scan solves it in n² time, and nobody had removed a polynomial factor from that since the problem was named.
The conjecture that all-pairs shortest paths on an n-vertex graph with polynomially bounded integer weights needs n^(3−o(1)) time — that shaving logarithmic factors is all anyone will ever get.
Running time O(n^(2−ε)) for some fixed ε > 0, as opposed to n²/polylog(n); the distinction is the whole point, because log-factor savings do not transfer through fine-grained reductions.
An algorithm that is always correct but whose running time is random, so the quoted bound is an expectation; weaker than deterministic, stronger than an algorithm that can return a wrong answer.

items.title: OpenSSH throws away the compression dictionary to close a channel leak
items.dek: OpenSSH 10.6, released on 6 October, disables the LZ77 dictionary stage of its optional zlib compression, because every channel multiplexed over one SSH connection shares a single 32-kilobyte compression history and can therefore emit back-references into another channel's plaintext.
items.why_it_matters: Compression ratio is now the price of isolation between channels: the Huffman stage survives and the dictionary does not, so a connection with compression enabled compresses noticeably worse under 10.6 than under 10.5. The alternative fix — one compression context per channel — would have traded the leak for a 32-kilobyte window per open channel instead, which is the kind of choice that only looks obvious once someone has written down what the shared state was actually buying.
items.background_md: DEFLATE, the algorithm inside zlib and gzip, compresses in two stages. LZ77 replaces a repeated byte string with a back-reference to an earlier copy inside a sliding window; Huffman coding then gives frequent symbols shorter codes. The first stage is what leaks. If an attacker can get a guess of their own compressed in the same window as a secret, a correct guess becomes a short back-reference and a wrong one stays literal bytes, so the output length answers the question. That is the mechanism behind CRIME and BREACH in TLS, and it is a property of compressing attacker data alongside secret data rather than of any cipher.
items.deeper_md:
RFC 4253 puts compression on the packet payload before the length field, the MAC and encryption, and SSH runs one compression context for the whole connection in each direction. Channel boundaries are therefore not compression boundaries: bytes sent on a forwarded port stay in the 32 KiB LZ77 window, available as match targets, until they scroll out.

Bäumer and Brinkmann's CCS 2026 paper turns that into an oracle. Each guess is padded so the compressed-length difference straddles an SSH block boundary, which amplifies a few bits into a multi-byte change in transmitted size — observable even though ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts the length field, by measuring bytes on the wire over a fixed window and averaging across repeats. In their cleanest case, Ansible, which enables compression and reuses one ControlMaster connection across tasks, an eight-character lowercase secret needed at most 276 guesses.

Scope, in the authors' own terms. Compression is off by default in OpenSSH; 4 of 33 surveyed clients prefer it; but 28.1M of 30.2M servers (93 %) advertise zlib during key exchange, and browser-driven variants still succeeded 67–69 % of the time under Chromium's private-network restrictions. They also say plainly that the joint occurrence of all preconditions in production is unmeasured, so nobody can say how many real connections were exposed. The same release raises default private-key KDF rounds from 24 to 32 and enables hybrid ML-DSA-44 with Ed25519 as a signature algorithm.

glossary.definition: The last 32 kilobytes of already-compressed input that DEFLATE keeps so it can replace a repeated string with a short pointer back into it; it is shared state, and shared state across security boundaries is the whole problem.

DEFLATE's second stage, which assigns shorter bit patterns to more frequent symbols; it compresses within one packet's symbol statistics and carries no cross-packet memory, which is why it can be kept.

Running several logical streams — a shell, a file transfer, forwarded TCP ports — inside one SSH connection; OpenSSH's ControlMaster does this automatically, and Ansible relies on it to avoid re-handshaking per task.

How many times a key-derivation function is iterated when encrypting a private key on disk; more rounds make each offline password guess proportionally more expensive, at a one-off cost when you unlock the key.

items.title: Rectify attention scores and some rows have nothing left to normalise
items.dek: Aryan Sood, Jaikaran Singh and Ishaan Bansal traced the failure of softpick — a replacement for attention's softmax that clips negative scores away — to initialisation, where every layer holds query rows whose every key scores negative and whose gradient norms reach 10¹² to 10¹⁴.
items.why_it_matters: Keeping the full denominator in the forward pass while backpropagating through only its positive half trains where plain softpick does not: at 230 million parameters the stop-gradient variant retrieves a passkey at 1,024 tokens of context perfectly and softpick retrieves nothing at any length. That locates the problem in the gradient rather than in rectification, which matters because rectification is the part that removes the outliers low-precision inference is paying for.
items.background_md: Attention weights a token by exponentiating a score and dividing by the sum over all tokens, which forces the weights to sum to one and so forces every token to receive a nonzero share whether or not anything wants it. Trained transformers cope by dumping the surplus onto a few fixed positions — attention sinks — and by growing a handful of hidden-state channels to roughly a hundred thousand times the typical magnitude. Both are harmless in 16-bit and expensive in 4-bit, because a quantiser's step size is set by the largest value it has to represent.
items.deeper_md:
Softpick replaces the exponentials with ReLU(e^(x−m) − e^(−m)) over a denominator of absolute values, which splits into D⁺, the sum over scores at or above the shift, and D⁻, the sum over those below it. The numerator depends only on D⁺.

At initialisation, with scores centred near zero, a query row can have every key land below the shift. Then D⁺ is exactly zero, the attention weight is zero for every key, and the Jacobian vanishes for all positions no matter which denominator the backward pass uses; near-dead rows blow up as 1/η as that sum approaches zero from above. All 12 layers contain such a row past the first token, with gradient norms between 10¹² and 10¹⁴. The stop-gradient operator keeps D⁺+D⁻ in the forward pass and routes the backward through D⁺ alone, so the backward pass divides by a denominator that is almost surely nonzero instead of by one going to zero.

At 230M, 30,000 steps on FineWeb-Edu at 8,192 context: loss 2.8569 against 2.9091, 23 dead heads of 238 against 29, and the passkey numbers above. It is worse on peak attention-weight kurtosis, 30.1M against 7.9M. The authors state the limits themselves — one checkpoint per operator, no seeds, no error bars, nothing above 340M, and a deliberately biased gradient estimator, so the closing gaps are two points consistent with a trend and not a demonstrated one.

glossary.definition: A token, usually the first, that trained attention heads send most of their weight to regardless of content; it exists because softmax must spend all of its probability mass somewhere.
A measure of how heavy a distribution's tails are relative to a Gaussian; high kurtosis in hidden states means a few enormous values set the numeric range the whole tensor must be quantised against.

A trick where the forward pass computes one expression and the backward pass pretends a different, simpler one was computed; it gives a gradient that is not the true derivative of the stated objective.
A test that buries a short random string in a long block of filler and asks the model to repeat it; it measures whether attention can reach far back at all, independently of language quality.

sources.title: Underscoring the Problem: Why Softpick Fails at Initialization

foundations.topic: P, NP, and what a reduction buys you
foundations.subtitle: How a proof that one problem is hard becomes a proof that a thousand are, and what that argument is worth on the day the one problem turns out to be easy.
foundations.tldr: Almost nobody proves a problem hard directly. Instead you prove that solving it would let you solve some already-notorious problem, which converts one piece of ignorance into a licence to stop trying on everything downstream. Today's Pulse has a preprint claiming to break two of those notorious problems at once, which is the right week to look at what that machinery actually promises — and what it quietly does not.

sections.heading: Easy to check is not easy to find
sections.body_md:
Start with the asymmetry everyone has felt. Given a completed Sudoku grid you can verify it in a minute by scanning rows, columns and boxes. Given a blank one you may be there all afternoon. **P** is the class of decision problems a deterministic machine settles in time bounded by a polynomial in the input size; **NP** is the class where a proposed answer comes with a certificate that can be *checked* in polynomial time. Every problem in P is in NP — checking is at most as hard as solving — and the question of whether the containment is strict is the one Stephen Cook and Leonid Levin independently formulated in 1971 and that the Clay Mathematics Institute put a prize on in 2000.

What makes it a real question rather than an obvious one is that nobody can exhibit a single problem in NP and prove it is not in P. Not one. Fifty-five years of work has produced no lower bound strong enough to separate the classes, which is why the whole field runs on conditional arguments instead.
sections.deeper_md: The definitions are machine-dependent in a way worth noticing. NP is usually introduced via non-deterministic Turing machines, which guess and then verify; the certificate formulation is equivalent and easier to use. The Cobham–Edmonds thesis, which equates "polynomial time" with "feasible", is the load-bearing and least defensible part of the setup: it classes an algorithm running in 10^100·n^1000 steps as feasible and one running in 1.0001^n as not, which is backwards for every input size anyone will ever see. The reason the field keeps the thesis anyway is that polynomial time is closed under composition — you can call a polynomial-time subroutine a polynomial number of times and stay inside the class — and that closure is exactly what makes reductions compose.

sections.heading: What a reduction actually is
sections.body_md:
A polynomial-time many-one reduction from problem X to problem Y is a function f, computable in polynomial time, such that an input x is a yes-instance of X exactly when f(x) is a yes-instance of Y. Write it X ≤ Y. The useful reading is mechanical: if you hand me a fast algorithm for Y, I now have a fast algorithm for X, because I translate and call yours.

The direction confuses almost everyone on first contact, and it is worth slowing down on. X ≤ Y says Y is *at least as hard* as X, because solving Y solves X. So to prove your new problem is hard you reduce a known-hard problem **to** it, not from it. Reducing your problem to a known-hard one proves nothing about yours — it only proves yours is no harder, which you probably suspected.

And the arrow carries information in both directions. Hardness flows forward from X to Y; speed flows backward from Y to X. The same construction that yesterday told you to give up on Y will, the moment someone cracks X, hand you an algorithm.
sections.deeper_md: There are weaker and stronger notions. A Turing (Cook) reduction may call the oracle for Y many times and post-process; many-one (Karp) reductions call it once and pass the answer through. For P-versus-NP purposes they behave similarly, but for finer distinctions — NP versus co-NP, or anything about counting — the difference matters, which is why the Karp form is the default. The thing to watch in any specific reduction is the *blow-up*: f maps an instance of size n to an instance of size g(n). For NP-completeness any polynomial g is fine. For the fine-grained statements in the fifth section, a reduction with g(n) = n² is useless, because an n^1.99 algorithm for Y then gives only n^3.98 for X, which is worse than what you had.

sections.heading: One expensive proof, then a great many cheap ones
sections.body_md:
Cook's 1971 theorem did one hard thing: it showed that Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete, meaning SAT is in NP and *every* problem in NP reduces to it. That proof is a direct simulation — it encodes the step-by-step operation of an arbitrary non-deterministic machine as a propositional formula, so a satisfying assignment is an accepting computation. Nothing since has had to do that again.

What happened next is the part worth learning from. Richard Karp's 1972 paper "Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems" gave polynomial-time reductions from satisfiability into a roster of ordinary combinatorial and graph problems, and by composition every one of them inherited NP-completeness. Karp's own account of how he got there is worth reading: he credits Jack Edmonds for the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial distinction, and Edmonds' min-max theorems as the thing that foreshadowed Cook's definition of NP.

That is the real product of a reduction web: leverage. Nobody re-derives Cook's theorem to classify a scheduling problem. They pick the nearest problem already on the list and build one encoding. Hardness results became routine, and the class grew to thousands of problems without anyone proving anything about machines again.
sections.deeper_md: The composition argument is the detail students skip. If every problem in NP reduces to SAT, and SAT reduces to clique, then every problem in NP reduces to clique by running the two translations in sequence — which is a polynomial-time computation because polynomials compose. That is why NP-completeness is contagious and why the list only grows. It is also why the list is a liability if its root is wrong: every one of those thousands of results is a conditional statement with the same antecedent, and a polynomial-time SAT algorithm would not weaken them one at a time, it would convert all of them simultaneously into polynomial-time algorithms. Hold that thought for the last section, where exactly this happens to a different root problem.

sections.heading: What NP-complete does not tell you
sections.body_md:
"NP-complete" is a statement about the worst case over all inputs of every size. It is not a statement about your inputs, and treating it as one is the most common practical error in the whole subject.

SAT is the cleanest demonstration, because SAT is both the root of the NP-completeness tree and an industrial technology. The SAT Competition runs every year — five tracks in the 2026 edition, with the benchmark instances tagged for download, per-instance scores published and solver sources released — and the entrants are the tools that hardware verification, scheduling and program analysis actually run on. Conflict-driven clause learning does not refute Cook's theorem. It exploits the fact that instances arising from real engineering carry structure, few genuinely independent decisions and dense implication chains, that an adversarially constructed instance would not have.

So the correct inference from "my problem is NP-complete" is narrow: stop looking for an algorithm fast on *every* instance, including the ones built to defeat you. It is not a reason to stop solving the instances you have. The usual next moves are a solver, an approximation with a proved ratio, a parameterised algorithm exponential only in some small structural quantity, or an average-case analysis.
sections.deeper_md: Each of those escape hatches has grown its own hardness theory, which is what keeps this from being mere optimism. Approximation has inapproximability results that fix, for particular problems, a ratio past which approximating is itself NP-hard, so "approximate it instead" is not a free pass. Parameterised complexity has its own completeness hierarchy for ruling out algorithms whose exponential part depends only on a chosen parameter. Average-case hardness is in the murkiest state of the three, and the standing evidence for that is negative: nobody knows how to build cryptography on NP-completeness, because worst-case and average-case hardness have resisted every attempt to connect them. The pattern repeats — each time someone proposes a way around a hardness result, the result reappears one level down, restated in the new setting.

sections.heading: Inside P, the same trick at a finer grain
sections.body_md:
Most problems an engineer meets are already in P, and "polynomial" is cold comfort when the polynomial is n³ and n is a hundred thousand. Fine-grained complexity applies the reduction trick one level down. Pick a handful of problems whose best known exponent has not budged — 3SUM, which asks whether three of n numbers sum to zero, at n²; all-pairs shortest paths at n³; CNF satisfiability at 2ⁿ — and *hypothesise* that those exponents are optimal. Then reduce them into everything else with reductions tight enough that the exponent survives the trip.

The pay-off is identical in shape and much sharper in resolution. Gajentaan and Overmars did this for computational geometry in 1995, building a web of problems that are quadratic-hard assuming 3SUM is; Pătraşcu extended it to data structures and dynamic graph problems. The APSP hypothesis, stated as "all-pairs shortest paths on n vertices with polynomially bounded integer weights requires n^(3−o(1)) time", carries its own web, and a STOC 2026 paper was still deriving equivalences from it in March.

Note the word *hypothesise*. These are conjectures held because nobody has beaten them, not theorems. That distinction is load-bearing and it is usually stated once and then forgotten.
sections.deeper_md: The reason to pick three roots rather than one is that nobody has shown them equivalent. There are reductions from 3SUM and from APSP into a shared middle layer — exact triangle, for instance, is hard under both — but no reduction from 3SUM to APSP or back, so each conjecture has to be assumed separately. That also means they can fail separately, and a result that refutes one leaves the others intact unless its technique happens to transfer. The *strong* exponential time hypothesis plays the same role for exponential-time problems and has been the most contested of the three, partly because it is the most specific: it pins down the base of the exponent, not just that one exists.

sections.heading: When the base problem falls
sections.body_md:
Which brings us to this week. The preprint in today's Pulse reports 3SUM in O(n^1.9992) and all-pairs shortest paths in O(n^2.9995), both deterministic, both truly subquadratic and subcubic in the sense that matters — a fixed polynomial saving, not shaved logarithms. If it holds, the two central hypotheses of fine-grained complexity are false, and so is the Exact Triangle hypothesis.

Watch what does and does not break. Every conditional lower bound stated as "hard unless 3SUM is easy" loses its antecedent and becomes vacuous. But the reductions are theorems and theorems do not expire; they simply start running the other way, delivering the new exponent to the problems they were built to constrain. The web was never a set of hardness proofs. It was a set of translations, and this week the thing being translated changed sign.

And hold the result at arm's length for now. It is days old, unrefereed, from two authors who built much of the theory it overturns, with constants the paper itself calls potentially impractical. The honest state is: a specific, checkable claim about one leaf-counting bound, and a field that is about to check it.
sections.deeper_md: The mechanism is worth a sentence because it is so narrow. Everything rests on computing a sparse subset of entries of a rectangular matrix product faster than writing the whole product down, built by recursing on Schönhage's identity — a 3×3 outer product and a 2×2 inner product in 10 multiplications instead of 13 — with the input encodings shared across blocks and the recursion tree pruned to the leaves the wanted entries touch. Only the *lopsided* regime benefits: tripartite graphs with two large parts and one part of size n^ε for ε below roughly 0.12. Balanced sparse triangle gets nothing. That is the shape of most progress here — a single primitive improves, and a hundred downstream exponents move by 0.0008.

glossary.definition: The decision problems a deterministic machine settles in a number of steps bounded by a polynomial in the input length; the class is closed under composition, which is the property that makes reductions chain together.
The decision problems whose yes-instances have a certificate checkable in polynomial time. It is about verification, not about randomness or parallelism, and it contains P.
A polynomial-time computable map f with x a yes-instance of X exactly when f(x) is a yes-instance of Y; it transfers hardness from X to Y and transfers speed from Y back to X.
In NP, and every problem in NP reduces to it. Satisfiability was the first, by direct simulation of a machine; everything since has been established by reduction from something already on the list.

How much larger a reduction makes the instance. Any polynomial is acceptable for NP-completeness; for fine-grained statements the blow-up must be close to linear or the exponent does not survive the translation.

Given n numbers, decide whether three sum to zero. Solvable in n² by sorting and scanning, and the assumed-optimal root of a large web of quadratic-hardness results in computational geometry and data structures.
Shorthand for "cubic up to subpolynomial factors": an algorithm may shave logarithms but not a fixed power. The APSP hypothesis is the claim that all-pairs shortest paths needs this much time.

The technique behind modern SAT solvers: when a search branch fails, derive a new clause explaining why and add it, so the same failure is never explored twice. It is why an NP-complete problem is routine in practice.

foundations.try_this: Run one reduction in both directions and watch the sign change. Open the Dagstuhl invited-talk paper, find where it names Pătraşcu's equivalence between 3SUM and 3SUM-Convolution, and write out — with the instance blow-up included — what a quadratic lower bound for one gives you for the other. Then open Theorem 2 of the Alman–Vassilevska Williams preprint, take the new O(n^1.9992) bound, and compute what exponent that equivalence now hands back to the convolution problem. Second half, about half an hour with a pen: write the reduction from 3-SAT to vertex cover yourself (two vertices per variable, three per clause is the standard construction) and measure how the instance grows as a function of formula size. If it grows faster than linearly, you have just shown yourself why a perfectly good NP-completeness proof is worth nothing as a fine-grained statement.
